18 Solo Photo Booth Ideas for Shooting Alone

With another person you are reacting. Alone you are performing, which is uncomfortable for almost everyone. Here is how to get around that.

Kishan Naik
August 1, 2026 6 min read

In this article

  1. Why solo feels harder, and what to do about it
  2. Six ideas that need nothing at all
  3. Six ideas with one object
  4. Six ideas built to repeat
  5. Setting up so you do not have to rush
  6. On not liking photos of yourself
  7. What to do with them

Taking a photo strip alone feels different, and most people notice it immediately. With another person there is someone to react to, someone to blame the silly frames on, and a shared understanding that this is a joke you are both in on. Alone, none of that exists. There is a lens, a countdown, and you.

That awkwardness is not a flaw in you. It is a structural consequence of removing the other person, and it goes away as soon as you replace what they were doing - which was giving you something to respond to.

This is a guide to shooting alone properly: 18 ideas, plus the setup and mindset that make a solo strip something you keep rather than delete.

Why solo feels harder, and what to do about it

In a shared session your expressions are reactions - to what they said, to how they looked, to the fact that frame two went wrong. You are not performing at the camera, you are responding to a person, and the camera happens to be there.

Alone, there is nothing to respond to, so you default to performing. Performing at a lens is uncomfortable for almost everyone and it shows in the result: the face is doing something deliberate and slightly frozen.

There are three fixes, and all of them work:

  • Give yourself a task. Something to do with your hands or your body means the face relaxes because it is no longer the main event.
  • Give yourself something to react to. Music, a video playing off to one side, a friend on a call who cannot see the booth.
  • Take more strips than you need. Strip one is always stiff. Strip three is you. This is the single most effective change and almost nobody does it.

The rule that matters most: take at least three strips in a row and only look at them afterwards. Reviewing between strips resets you back to self-conscious every time.

Six ideas that need nothing at all

1The four directions

Look left, look right, look down, look at the lens. No expression required. The variety comes from the geometry, and it is impossible to do badly.

2Getting closer

Start far from the camera and move in one step per frame. By frame four you are uncomfortably close. Simple, and it creates a sense of momentum a static strip never has.

3The slow turn

Begin facing fully away. Rotate a quarter turn per frame. Frame four is straight down the lens. Reliably the most cinematic solo strip you can produce.

4Eyes closed, then open

Three frames with your eyes shut, the fourth open. The contrast is startling and the closed-eye frames are unexpectedly peaceful.

5Hands

Hands in your hair, over your face, under your chin, at your neck. Gives the frames structure without requiring any facial expression at all.

6The genuine laugh

Play something that reliably makes you laugh and start the countdown a few seconds before the funny part. Frames two and three will be real, and a real laugh outperforms every posed expression.

Six ideas with one object

7The book you are actually reading

Not a prop book - the one on your bedside table. In two years the specific title will be the detail that dates the strip and brings the whole period back.

8Your coffee

The most honest solo portrait available. A mug, a normal morning, a face that has not yet fully woken up.

9A mirror at an angle

Held so the strip catches your face twice from two directions. Looks far more considered than it is.

10A single flower

Held to the lens, tucked behind an ear, half-covering your face. It fills a frame that would otherwise be mostly empty background.

11Today's outfit

A deliberate outfit record. Full length if the camera allows, otherwise from the shoulders. People take these constantly on their phones and almost never keep them properly - a strip does.

12Something that will not exist in a year

The lanyard from a job you are leaving, the keys to a flat you are moving out of, a cast about to come off. These strips get more valuable at a rate nothing else on this list matches.

Six ideas built to repeat

Solo strips are where a repeating tradition works best, because there is nobody else to coordinate with. You cannot be stood up by yourself.

13The monthly self-portrait

Same day each month. Same position if you can manage it. Twelve of these is a year of your own face, and it will show you things about that year you did not notice while living it.

14The haircut record

One strip immediately before, one immediately after. Over several years this becomes an unexpectedly precise timeline.

15End of a project

Every time you finish something - a piece of work, a course, a difficult month - one strip. A record of endings, which is a thing almost nobody documents.

16The same chair

One fixed position in your home, revisited. The room changes around you. You change in it. Both are visible.

17Birthday, every year

Same pose, same framing, once a year. The most obvious idea here and the one people are most consistently glad they started.

18The bad day strip

Counterintuitive, and worth considering. A strip on a genuinely difficult day is uncomfortable to take and quietly valuable later - it is honest in a way a camera roll of good days is not. Nobody has to see it.

Setting up so you do not have to rush

The scramble to get into position after pressing start is the main reason first frames are bad. Fifteen seconds of setup removes it entirely.

  • Get the camera to eye level. A laptop on a desk points up your nose. Stack it on books until the lens is level with your eyes. This one change improves a solo strip more than any other.
  • Face a window. Not with your back to it - that silhouettes you. Facing it gives soft, even light across your whole face.
  • Clear the background. You are the only subject, so anything else in frame competes. A plain wall is fine; a plain wall with one plant is better.
  • Sit or stand back further than feels right. Solo strips are usually cropped too tight. Some space around you looks intentional.
  • Check the countdown length first. Know how long you have before it starts, so you are not still moving on frame one.

The lighting side of this matters more than anything else and is covered fully in the lighting guide. If your webcam looks worse than you expect, the webcam quality guide covers the fixes.

On not liking photos of yourself

Worth addressing directly, because it is the actual reason many people never take a solo strip.

There is a well-documented reason your own photographs look wrong to you. You see your face reversed in mirrors thousands of times, and mere exposure makes the familiar version feel correct. A photograph shows you the unreversed version - the one everyone else has always seen. It is not worse. It is just unfamiliar, and unfamiliar reads as wrong.

A photo strip helps with this more than a single photo, for a specific reason: four frames in sequence show your face moving. You are much more likely to recognise yourself in a sequence than in a still, because motion is how people actually know each other.

The other thing that helps is volume. Take ten strips over a month and the discomfort fades noticeably - not because you look better, but because you become familiar to yourself in a form other than a mirror.

You do not have to show anyone. A solo strip can be entirely private, and some of the best ones are.

What to do with them

Solo strips accumulate quietly and then, at some point, become the most interesting thing in your files. A folder called "monthly" with eighteen strips in it is a genuinely unusual object - most people have thousands of photos of everywhere they went and almost none of what they looked like while they were living there.

Print them in batches rather than individually. Twelve strips printed at once, dated on the back, in a small envelope, is one of the cheapest good things you can make. The process is in how to print photo strips at home, and what to do with your photo strips has more on keeping them.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I take a good photo strip alone?

Give yourself a task rather than a pose, put something on that you will react to, and take at least three strips in a row without looking at them in between. The first strip is always stiff and the third is usually the one you keep - reviewing between strips resets you to self-conscious every time.

Why do I look worse in photos than in the mirror?

You see your face reversed in mirrors thousands of times, and repeated exposure makes that version feel correct. A photograph shows the unreversed version everyone else has always seen. It is not worse, only unfamiliar - and a four-frame strip helps because motion is how people actually recognise faces.

Where should I put the camera for a solo photo strip?

At eye level, which usually means stacking a laptop on books. A camera below eye level points up at your nose and is the most common reason solo strips disappoint. Also sit further back than feels natural - solo strips are almost always cropped too tightly.

What can I do in a solo photo strip without props?

Look in four different directions, move a step closer each frame, rotate a quarter turn per frame so you end up facing the lens, or shoot three frames with your eyes closed and open them for the fourth. All four rely on geometry rather than expression, so they are hard to do badly.

Is it strange to take photos of yourself?

No, and it produces something most people are missing. Most camera rolls hold thousands of photos of places and almost none of what the owner looked like while they were living there. A monthly solo strip fills that gap, and it does not have to be shown to anyone.

How do I take photobooth-style photos at home by myself?

Open an online photobooth in your browser, place your laptop or phone at eye level, and face a soft light source like a window or lamp. The automated countdown timer lets you prepare between frames without rushing to click the shutter.
